result.abstractText:
Objective

To evaluate whether ultrasonography (US) detects early-stage knee osteoarthritis (OA) more effectively than conventional radiography (CR) in a population representing primary and occupational healthcare, and to assess associations between imaging findings and symptoms.

Design

In this cross-sectional study, 315 subjects (60% women; mean age 49 years, range 21-63 years) with knee symptoms underwent knee US and CR, resulting in assessment of 345 knees. Ultrasonographic evaluation included effusion, synovial hypertrophy, osteophytes, femoral cartilage damage, meniscal pathology, and protrusion, from which a composite US sum score was constructed. Radiographic severity was graded using the Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) scale (grade 0, n = 128; grade 1, n = 90; grade 2, n = 78; grade 3, n = 38; grade 4, n = 11). WOMAC questionnaires were completed prior to imaging. Statistical analyses included Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney tests, univariate analyses, and Pearson correlation coefficients.

Results

US detected more osteophytes than CR, particularly at the femoral margins, while tibial osteophyte detection was comparable between modalities. US identified more femoral cartilage damage than CR-detected joint-space narrowing. Meniscal protrusion was associated with radiographic joint-space narrowing and KL grade (p < 0.001). Effusion size and synovial hypertrophy increased with higher KL grades (p < 0.001). The US sum score correlated with KL grade (r = 0.73, p < 0.001). Both the US sum score and KL grade showed modest associations with WOMAC scores.

Conclusions

US detects more structural abnormalities than CR in early-stage knee OA. While ultrasonographic findings correlate with radiographic severity, their associations with clinical symptoms remain limited, supporting US as a complementary tool for structural assessment in knee OA.
